extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, biologists, and educated readers of natural history
extracted.subtask_description: Assessment and explanation of the explanatory power and objections to Darwin's theory of descent with modification by natural selection, with emphasis on embryology, rudimentary organs, classification, sterility, variability, and the fossil record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance at corresponding ages
rubrics_metrics.description: Variations which appear at a certain age in parents tend to appear at the corresponding age in their offspring (though not invariably).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin uses measurements of puppies, foals, and pigeons to show that many breed-differences appear late and are inherited at the same late age. Exceptions (e.g., the short-faced tumbler pigeon) are noted and discussed as cases where differences must have appeared earlier or been inherited earlier. This principle is posed as a key to explaining embryological facts and the relative similarity of embryos among related species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Late-appearing modifications explain embryonic similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: If successive slight variations have supervened at a rather late age and been inherited at a corresponding late age, the young of newly formed species will resemble one another much more closely than the adults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained via examples (pigeons, fore-limbs becoming hands/paddles/wings) and by contrasting embryo vs adult modification. Used to justify why embryonic structures reveal ancestral patterns and are important for classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early-appearing or early-inherited modifications produce adult-like embryos
rubrics_metrics.description: If successive steps of variation supervene at a very early period of life, or each step is inherited at an earlier period than it first appeared, the young or embryo will closely resemble the mature parent-form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contingency accounts for groups (cuttle-fish, spiders, some insects like Aphis) whose embryos closely resemble adults. Darwin treats this as an alternative explanation and acknowledges it as a normal outcome in certain lineages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of use and disuse acting chiefly on mature individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Influence of long-continued exercise (use) or disuse mainly affects the mature animal and these effects tend to be inherited at a corresponding mature age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to explain why embryonic structures remain less modified: the young haven't experienced the same use/disuse. This supports why adult specialization may not be reflected in embryos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embryonic structure reveals progenitor (classification criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The embryo, being in a less modified state, reveals the structure of its progenitor; embryonic characters are therefore especially important for classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues that similarity in embryonic stages indicates common descent even when adult structures differ widely; he cites cirripede larvae recognized as crustacean and states that classification should be genealogical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudimentary/atrophied/aborted organs as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of rudimentary, atrophied, or aborted organs (vestiges) throughout nature bears the stamp of inutility and indicates former functions and descent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include rudimentary mammæ in male mammals, ‘bastard-wing’ as a digit, rudiments of pelvis in snakes, teeth in fetal whales, and wings reduced under wing-cases. Darwin argues these are intelligible under descent with modification but puzzling under special creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudiments often retain potentiality and vary
rubrics_metrics.description: Rudimentary organs sometimes retain the ability to develop (potentiality) and can vary in degree among individuals and closely allied species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: male mammary glands occasionally develop and secrete milk; rudimentary teats in Bos sometimes become developed; petals or stamens sometimes appear as rudiments or develop fully. Crosses (Kölreuter) show increase of rudiment size in hybrids, indicating homology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organs may become rudimentary for one function but retained for another
rubrics_metrics.description: An organ serving two purposes may become rudimentary or aborted for one purpose while remaining efficient for the other, or be co-opted to a new function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: male florets with a pistil rudimentary in stigma but retaining style for brushing pollen; swim-bladder becoming a nascent lung in some fish. Demonstrates how natural selection and modification can change function gradually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudimentary parts are relatively larger in embryos
rubrics_metrics.description: A rudimentary part or organ is generally of greater size relatively to adjoining parts in the embryo than in the adult; embryos thus often show less rudimentary conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to explain why embryonic remains of lost structures (teeth, limbs) are detectable even when absent in adults; ties into inheritance at corresponding ages and timing of reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of rudimentary organs by disuse and selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Rudimentary organs originate mainly by disuse, leading to gradual reduction over successive generations, aided by natural selection when organs become injurious or useless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites eyes in cave animals, wings of island birds, and domestic examples (tailless breeds, earless breeds) as illustrating reduction by disuse; economy of growth may also eliminate unused materials, leading to obliteration of rudiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modification via innumerable slight steps is plausible
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex organs and instincts can be perfected by accumulation of innumerable slight variations, each beneficial to the individual, provided gradations exist, variability exists, and there is a struggle for existence preserving advantageous deviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin frames these three propositions as prerequisites for natural selection to account for complex adaptations. He acknowledges difficulty in tracing exact gradations but invokes Natura non facit saltum and many observed gradations in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sterility of first crosses vs hybrids explained by constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost universal sterility of species when first crossed is incidental on constitutional differences in reproductive systems and is not a special endowment; varieties are more fertile when crossed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin contrasts first crosses (fertile in varieties) with hybrids (often sterile due to compounded organizations). Reciprocal crosses yielding different results support constitutional explanations; domestication tends to reduce sterility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fertility trends with degree of modification
rubrics_metrics.description: Lesser changes in conditions of life and crosses between less modified forms increase vigour and fertility, whereas considerable changes and crosses between greatly modified forms tend to lessen fertility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to explain why varieties (less modified) are generally fertile inter se, while hybrids and greatly modified crosses show reduced fertility. Also relates to observed increased vigour from crossing slightly modified forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical distribution must account for migration and extinction
rubrics_metrics.description: On descent with modification all related species must have spread from ancestral localities to their present ranges, so migration, extinction, and long time intervals must be invoked to explain distribution patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes ignorance of all migration means but points to long time spans, glacial periods, and intermittent formations as facilitating distribution; broken ranges may reflect extinction in intermediate areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfection of the geological record explains absence of intermediate fossils
rubrics_metrics.description: The geological record is far more imperfect than generally admitted; intermittent deposition, taphonomic bias, limited fossilizable classes, extinction of intermediates, and long blank intervals account for the rarity of intermediate links.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues that only a tiny portion of past life is fossilized and preserved; intermediate varieties will often be supplanted and extinct; widely ranging species and local varieties patterns reduce fossil detectability. This is the main counter to objections about missing links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate forms often supplanted and thus rarely preserved
rubrics_metrics.description: Intermediate varieties that initially exist in intermediate zones are liable to be supplanted by the allied forms on either hand, and so are less likely to persist or be found in the fossil record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin explains that allied forms existing in greater numbers will be modified faster and replace intermediate varieties; consequentially, fossil evidence for connecting links will be scarce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability under domestication and persistence of inherited modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Under domestication organisms show much variability (reproductive systems being susceptible to conditions), modifications can be inherited for long periods, and domestication tends to eliminate sterility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin uses domestic examples to infer the capacity for variability in nature: correlation of growth, use/disuse, and physical conditions govern variability; once a modification is inherited for many generations it may persist indefinitely under stable conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification must use descent (genealogical arrangement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural system of classification is genealogical: taxa should be arranged according to descent, with grades of acquired difference reflected in varieties, species, genera, families, orders, and classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin says descent is the 'hidden bond' naturalists seek and explains why embryological and rudimentary characters are valuable for determining affinities. He advises extending the element of descent in classification.
